charles-haynes-1880-07-31.A1:
Negro Killed.
Nashville, July 31—The American's M'Kenzie special says B. W. Moore, an attorney, shot and mortally wounded Charles Haynes, colored. Haynes had interrupted Moore in a speech delivered at a barbecve in Weakley county a few days ago. He had also threatened Moore's life. Moore spoke to him about it, when Haynes became angry and seized a stick which Moore had in his hand. Moore commanded him to let it loose. Haynes refused and wrenched it from Moore's hand, when Moore shot him. Moore gave himself up. Haynes is a turbulent character.
charles-haynes-1880-07-31.A2:
POLETICAL NOTES.
COLONEL H. B. HAYS, a wealthy citizen of Pittsburg, denies the report that he will support Hancock.

EX-SENATOR LEWIS of Virginia was in the city yesterday. He feels very confident that the republicans will gain several members of congress in his state and secure the electoral vote for Garfield.

A MCKENZIE, Tenn., negro interrupted B. W. Moore, who was making a speech. The latter treasured up the wrong, and meeting the African, next-day, got into an altercation with him, in the course of which he shot him fatally.

THERE is some hope now that the differences that have sprung up between the republicans of the first Minnesota congressional district will be amicably adjusted. The matter has been referred to the central committee of the state.

A GENTLEMAN who has traveled through central and western New York during the past fortnight gives a glowing account of the movements of the republicans. The enthusiasm of the people is constantly increasing and the work of organization is being prosecuted with unusual vigor. He regards New York as certain for Garfield by more than 20,000 majority.

The mass meeting at Woodstock, Va., on Saturday for the purpose of inaugurating a movement for the consolidation of the funders and readjusters' electoral tickets, appears to have been a distressing failure. It was not countenanced by the presence of any party leader on either side; the committee on arrangements found it impossible to secure speakers of any political prominence, and all that could be done was to get a few signatures to a petition to the state executive committees of both wings, asking them to bring about a compromise on the basis of allowing the funders and readjusters each to name five electors on the new ticket and the national democratic committee to pick out the eleventh man.
charles-haynes-1880-07-31.A3:
CARROLL ITEMS.
The democracy had a big barbecue at Hico, Carroll county, last Thursday, at which Gen. Atkins, Capt. R. P. Cole, and A. G. Hawkins, Esq., delivered eloquent speeches. There were about fifteen hundred people on the ground, and many friends were made for Hancock and reform.

On Wednesday of last week B. W. Moore, Esq., became involved in a difficulty with a negro named Chas Hayes, in M'Kenzie, in which the latter was fatally shot in the abdomen. The trouble grew out of some interruptions made by Hayes while Moore was delivering a speech at a barbecue a few days before. The negro had afterward boasted of it and, we learn, also threatened Moore's life. When they met, Moore talked to him about it, when the negro tried to take a stick from him. Moore told him to turn it loose, or he would shoot him. After a short struggle, Moore fired, with the above result. Hayes had the reputation of being a desperate man. Since the foregoing was written the negro has died and Moore left the country.

From the Huntingdon Vindicator.

Custer, the man who shot and killed the negro at McKenzie last week, has not yet been captured. Both were Republicans.

Rev. Charles Moore, a colored minister of much prominence in this county, has publicly declared his intention to vote for Hancock and English.
There is not a young man in Huntingdon who makes any pretention towards christianity. If ever a revival of religion was ever needed in the world, it is in this town.

dr-wiley-w-williams-mechanicsburg-1880-0.A1:
Paid to Kill a Man In Yazoo.
YAZOO CITY, Miss., July 26.—Dr. N. F. Williams, of Mechanicsburg, was assassinated on Saturday evening while riding home. His horse came home riderless, and and a search being made the Doctor's body was found. A negro was arrested on suspicion, and has since confessed his guilt. He says he was paid to kill the Doctor.
dr-wiley-w-williams-mechanicsburg-1880-0.A2:
Murder in Yazoo County.
On Friday night last, as Dr. Wiley T. Williams, of Mechanicsburg, Yazoo county, was returning home, he was waylaid and assassinated by some party there unknown. On Monday, a negro, and a white man by the name of Louis Rosenberg, living in Mechanicsburg, were arrested on suspicion, and were taken to Satartia for trial. The negro confessed to the killing, and said that Louis Rosenberg gave him one hundred and fifty dollars to kill Dr. Williams. A large crowd soon gathered, prepared to lynch the prisoners, but through the adroitness of the Deputy Sheriff, Mr. Frank Wilson, the prisoners were conveyed safely across the Yazoo river and a guard placed over the ferryboat, and the infuriated lynchers were prevented from doing their work. The crowd was still upon the bank of the river, when the steamer Carrol passed down. Dr. Williams was a native of Warren county, and was much esteemed and respected in the neighborhood in which he resided. He leaves a wife and ten children.—Vicksburg Commercial.
dr-wiley-w-williams-mechanicsburg-1880-0.A3:
property taxpayers of the town are willing to submit to a special tax in aid of a railroad to be constructed from Monroe through Bastrop to some point near the Arkansas line. The Mayor has ordered the election to be held on the 17th of August. It is proposed to levy a tax of 5 mills on the dollar per annum on the taxable property of the town for a period not to exceed ten years.

A fire at Caribon, Me., recently, destroyed the engine house, two engines and other property belonging to the New Brunswick railway. Loss, $25,000; insurance unascertained.

Pat Malony, a laborer, while drunk in Houston, Texas, laid on the street car track. A car loaded with passengers was driven about an hour after. The verdict at the inquest attached no blame to the company.

The Sheriffs of Texas held a state convention yesterday.

Robt. Scott, colored, of Austin, Texas, was shot and instantly killed by another colored individual Tuesday evening.

A dispatch from Youngstown, Ohio, says a captive balloon at that place. well inflated, while up with a man and woman from the country in it, broke loose Tuesday, ascended to a great height and disappeared in a northeasterly direction. Dispatches were sent ahead to keep a lookout for it. It was feared it world drift into the lake.

Col. Ed. Richardson, the largest cotton planter in the United States, is favorably spoken of by the press of Mississippi, as a suitable candidate for Governor, at the next State election.

Dr. Wiley T. Williams, of Mechanicsburg, Yazoo county, Miss., was waylaid and assassinated by some unknown party on Friday night 23d ult. A negro and a white man who live in Mechanicsburg were arrested on suspicion, and taken to Satartia for trial. The negro confessed to the killing, and said that the white man gave him one hundred and fifty dollars to kill the Doctor. A large crowd soon gathered, prepared to lynch the prisoners, but through the adroitness of the deputy sheriff, the prisoners were conveyed safely across the Yazoo river, and a guard placed over the ferryboat, and the infuriated lynchers were foiled in their plans.

The colored starving Kansas exodusters have appealed to the Texans for money to get back. Jeff. Grimes has gone North with funds to bring back 500 of them.

There were 586 births, 101 marriages and 641 deaths in New York city last week.
dr-wiley-w-williams-mechanicsburg-1880-0.A6: Dr. W. T. Williams, a merchant at Mechanicsburg, Yazoo county, was waylaid and killed near that village on the night of the 24th ult. Tobe Bell, a negro, was arrested on suspicion and confessed to being guilty of the crime, but claimed to have been paid to murder Dr. Williams, by L. Rosenberg, Jr. another merchant of Mechanicsburg. Rosenberg was arrested and taken to Yazoo City, but the sheriff learning that he was closely followed by a mob from the Satartia and Mechanicsburg neighborhood, sent him to Canton for safety. Rosenberg reached here in custody of Messrs. Frank Wilson and Robt. Bell, deputy sheriffs of Yazoo county. A telegram from the sheriff of Yazoo caused the prisoner to be taken back to Yazoo City after he had been here about 24 hours. We have not heard the result of Rosenberg's examination.
dr-wiley-w-williams-mechanicsburg-1880-0.A9: The preliminary examination of the parties charged with the assassination of Dr. Williams of Yazoo county, has been finished with the following result: Tobe Bell colored, and Louis Rosenberg white, were committed to jail, without bail, and Mike Rosenberg and Fred Sturdivant were allowed bail in the sums of fifteen hundred dollars and two hundred and fifty dollars respectively.

Curious mistakes sometimes happen at funerals. An Italian, whose wife died, was so overwhelmed that his friends didn't let him go to the funeral, but sent him to spend the day in the country. He came home late in the evening and found his wife's body in grave clothes, still lying in his bedroom awaiting interment. He rushed to tell the police, who at first thought he was crazy, but on investigation found that the undertaker had forgotten the corpse, and nailed up the empty coffin, and that the latter had been buried with the usual ceremonies.

CINCINNATI, O., July 26.—A colored Baptist camp meeting, ten miles south of Hillsboro, Ohio, was the scene, on Friday night and Sunday afternoon, of a bloody fight. On Friday night a party of drunken roughs went to camp about 10 o'clock and began an attack with pistols, clubs and stones. They were repulsed, and William Dickman. one of their number, was shot through the abdomen. On Sunday afternoon a party said to number two hundred, attacked the camp and a most desperate fight followed, ending in the breaking up of the meeting. It is thought some of the colored people were killed, but they dispersed so rapidly that facts could not be gathered. No arrests have been made.

The Rev. George T. McClelland went from Pittsburgh to Reynoldsville, Pa, to conduct revival meetings in a Presbyterian church. He was quartered in Elder Kelso's house. The neighbors heard the noise of a fight in the building, and presently the clergyman was chased out by the elder, who kicked him violently at every step. Mr. McClelland subsequently said: Mrs. Kelson invited me to kiss her, and I did so. Then her husband assailed me. I wish now that I hadn't kissed her."

A special to the Bay City (Mich.) Tribune states that H. Mellen's saw mill, at Bagley, Otsego county, blew up Wednesday afternoon, killing two men and seriously injuring several others. The owner of the mill is among the injured.

Joseph Staats, a young man who was married only nineteen days ago, was shot dead in his yard, at Centralia, Ill., on Sunday night of last week, by some unknown person. It is thought by some to be a suicide, while others believe it to be a murder.

Early Wednesday morning, Thomas Delano was found on State street, Chicago, with his stomach cut open, and in a dying condition. A woman named Minnie Dixon has been arrested on her own confession. The motive for the crime is unknown.

hillsboro-hillsboro.A4: A COUPLE of weeks ago the colored folks had a camp meeting over in Highland county, and a lot of ruffians broke the meeting up. There was a general battle, firearms being used. Women and children, in wagons, were shot while passing through a village called Danville. Let us send more missionaries to Africa!
hillsboro-hillsboro.A6: St. Louis Republican:—The breaking up of a colored people's camp-meeting at Danville, Ohio, lately was a bloody affair, and it is supposed cost several lives. A small party of white "roughs" loaded with whisky made the first attempt to break up the camp, but were driven back by the colored brethren and sisters, all of whom showed fight and defended the church militant. The next day the camp was attacked by a mob of about two hundred, armed with pistols, shot guns, rifles and carbines. This force was too strong for the camp-meeting and the colored worshippers fled for their lives. Several wagon-leads of them were fired into, and, it is said, some were killed. A large number were wounded, and the deserted camp ground looked more like a battle-field than a place of worship. This was an outrage upon negroes in the loyal state of Ohio—Ohio is supposed to be truly loyal. If it had occurred in one of the Southern states, what fuel it might have made to fire the Northern Republican heart in the presidential campaign. In the State of Hayes and Garfield it is another matter of a different color.

dleton, Conn., Savings bank, on the 27th, over $20,000 in gold bonds, and $40,000 State of South Carolina bonds, on which not much value is put, were taken. The cash belonged to the bank and the bonds to individuals, who had deposited them in the vault.

ISAIAH CARR, in Kent county, R. I., jail, awaiting examination on a charge of killing his nephew, was found dead in his cell on the 28th.

A DISPATCH from Denison, Texas, dated the 28th, says: "To-day near Gobson station, I. T., a party of Creeks attacked two Cherokees, and killed one and wounded the other. Two Creeks were hanged by the Cherokees Monday night, hence the reprisal."

THOMAS DELANA was fatally stabbed by his paramour in a Chicago restaurant on the 27th.

Three or four men entered the Middletown Savings bank, Conn., during the absence at dinner of some of the officials, and, engaging the clerks in conversation, accomplices robbed the vault of $8,500.

MICHAEL MADDOX killed John Schaba, a Bohemian, in the northeastern section of Baltimore, on the 27th. Maddox alleges that he found Schaba in his (Maddox's) wife's chamber.

On the 27th Mrs. Anna Lynch, of the Keystone house, Portland, Oregon, fatally stabbed Alex. Mattieson, who, she claims, made a dishonorable proposition and attempted an indecent assault.

JOSEPH ENEAS, alias Hoffman, an American resident in Aspinwall, Panama, and claiming to be a merchant, was arrested on charge of putting into circulation counterfeit greenback United States notes. Hoffman figured prominently in Brooklyn papers in 1877, when his swindlings were stated at some $60,000.

GEORGE BELL and Cleary, old offenders, were arrested at New York on the 27th, on charge of passing five counterfeit chicks on the National Bank of Baltimore and the Merchants' Bank of the same city, and obtaining $10,000.

JOHN DROGS, the negro who outraged Mrs. James T. Chiffels on the 24th, near Durnestown, Md., was lodged in jail at Rockwell on the 26th. Shortly before 4 o'clock next morning about 50 men appeared at the jail and after a sharp melee with the officers, took the ravisher out and hung him. Duggs made a full confession of his crime to the sheriff previous to the jail being forced.

Ar an early hour on the 27th, one of two burglaries was shot and killed while attempting an entrance to the residence of Hon. D. N. Solomon, on the latter's farm, about thirty miles from Council Bluffs, Ia., on the Wabash road. The fatal shot was fired by B. L. Solomon. The name of the dead burgher is not known:

Joseph Staats, a young man, was shot dead in his yard at Centrailla, Ill., on the night of the 15th, by some person unknown.

Harmon McCoy, living four miles from Arcola, Ill., was stabbed and killed by Elisha McCabe aided by Joel Engel, during a quarrel, on the 25th. McCabe escaped, but Engle was arrested.

A colored murderer hailed George Washington was hung by a mob in the backwoods of Tennessee recently.

A colored camp meeting near Hillsboro, O., was broken up on the 25th, by a gang of roughs, who commenced operations by attempting to demolish the sutler's tent and ended by tiring into the crowd. Three persons were badly, probably fainly injured, while several others were considerably hurt.

Pat Kelly and Jack Brown, of Rochester, Pa., have been on bad terms for two years. They met on the 25th and resolved on finding out who was the best man. Brown was badly beaten, and acknowledged that he was. Enraged at his being whipped, and after the fight was all over, he pulled out his revolver, and, remarking that Kelly would never again whip anybody, fired three shots at him in quick succession. It is believed that Kelly will die of the wounds.

Is Oakland, Cal., on the 26th, Edward Schreder entered the office of Dr. Alfred Schreder being teller of the Linden and San Francisco bank of Oakland, and Lefevre a long established and popular dentist. Suspicion of criminal intimacy between the murdered man and Schroeder's wife led to the tragedy.

Mrs. Edward Geason, wife of a prominent merchant and old citizen of Dayton, O., committed suicide on the 25th by taking poison.

Dr. M. F. Williams, of Mechanicsburg, Miss., was assassinated while riding home on the night of the police. Morton was taken to jail and several deputy sheriffs placed on guard. A crowd soon gathered, overpowered the guard and lynched the prisoner.

Mrs. Edward Geason, wife of a prominent merchant and old citizen of Dayton, O., committed suicide on the 25th by taking poison.

Dr. M. F. Williams, of Mechanicsburg, Miss., was assassinated while riding home on the night of the 24th. His horse reached home riderless and search being made the doctor's body was found. A negro was arrested on suspicion and has since confessed his guilt. He says he was paid to kill the doctor.

At Sag Harbor, N. Y., on the 26th, Miles Morris was shot dead by a seaman who accused Morris of being improperly intimate with his wife.

Charles Morton shot Policeman O'Neil at Eokomo, Col., on the afternoon of the 25th. Morton was intoxicated and raising a disturbance in a saloon, the policeman attempted to arrest him and was shot dead. Morton was taken to jail and several deputy sheriffs placed on guard. A crowd soon gathered, overpowered the guard and lynched the prisoner.

H. P. Comegys, stenographer of the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe railroad office at Topeka, Ks., suicided on the 25th.

A dispatch from Winnepeg says while Constable Powers was crossing Red river with Mike Carroll, an escaped prisoner, Carroll upset the boat and both were drowned.

Fred Welcom was arrested at Cheyenne on the 24th for murdering John F. Turner, son of Sheriff Turner, of Utah county, in Echo Canon, Utah, July 12. Welcom confesses and gives the name of an accomplice. The murder was for theft and was extremely brutal.

On the 24th, Wm. Carnes, a farmer living four miles cast of Vanastyne, Texas, was shot and instantly killed by W. R. Lance, his neighbor.

Abraham Martin attacked his wife with an axe at Abbeville, S. C., on the 24th instant, inflicting fatal wounds. He became enraged because his wife upbraided him for infidelity.

The Highland News. HILLSBOROUGH, OHIO. THURSDAY, - - AUGUST 26: 1880 JAMES A. BARFIELD CHESTER A. ABBY WILK
Our Candidate for Congress, the Hon. Alphonso Hart.

We have only time to say, as our paper is just going to press, that the Republican Congressional Convention of this district, which has just adjourned, met the general expectation and wishes of the Republicans of the district, by placing in nomination our townsman, Ex-Lt. Gov. Alphonso Hart. Gov. Hart, though he did not seek the nomination, now that he has accepted it, will go into the canvass with all the energy of his nature, and if he does not achieve victory, in the face of the heavy majority against him, he will at least spare no honorable endeavor to deserve it. Let every true Republican heartily second his efforts, and he will come out of the contest, if not triumphant, at least bearing the standard so gallantly as to reflect honor upon himself and the district.

We shall take a future occasion to give our readers a sketch of our candidate's past history and public life, which will prove that he is worthy of the high and honorable position in which he has been placed by the unanimous voice of his fellow-Republicans.

AN ALABAMA "ARGUS,"

WHOSE HUNDRED EYES MAKE IT SEE PLAINLY

WHAT IS NOT TO BE SEEN.

THE DANVILLE CAMP MEETING DISTURBANCE

CHARGED TO OHIO REPUBLICANS, AND USED

TO FRIGHTEN ALABAMA COL-ORED VOTERS.

A FEW SOLID FACTS FOR THE ARGUS TO DIGEST,

WHICH MAY MAKE IT MORE CAREFUL IN FUTURE.

The Selma (Ala.) Argus is a Democratic paper, of course. We say "of course," because under the system of "a free ballot and a full and fair count," so beautifully advocated by Gen. Hancock in his letter of acceptance, and so charmingly illustrated by his followers, in the late so-called "election" (!) in that State, it has become so extremely unhealthy for Republican newspapers that only three are reported in Rowell's Newspaper Directory for 1880; and secondly, because the columns of the Argus furnish abundant and unimpeachable proof of its "Democracy," of the most modern, approved, patent back action, Southern brand.

A copy of the Argus of Aug. 6th, has been sent us by a friend, and one of the first editorial articles which struck our astonished gaze was headed thus: "The Negro in Ohio!" Curious to learn what our colored brother had been doing, on the principle of "going from home to hear the news," we read on as follows:

"It occurred in this loyal home of loyalists par excellence, after this fashion. The negroes in the vicinity of Danville, in that State, and, we believe, in Highland county, devotional, as is the wont of the race, have camp-grounds, whereon they proposed to meet and worship God in peace beneath their own vine and fig-tree. They came together from all the country round about, and for a week there was song and prayer

and praise and peace and joy and happiness. But there was also dissatisfaction. White people thereabouts, Republicans most certainly, who are greatly distressed about the condition of the negroes 'way down South,' and are anxious that they should be protected here by the strong arm of the government in the enjoyment of rights nowhere denied to them, but who think they should stay where they belong, or should go to Indiana or some other State where their votes are more needed, concluded that religious enjoyments were altogether too good for these brethren and sisters of the colored persuasion, and determined to put an end to their exercises. Whereupon these fair-skinned political negrophilists armed and equipped themselves with forty rounds of Cincinnati whisky, intruded themselves upon the camp-grounds, and kicked up a truly 'loil muss, from which, however, they emerged second-best. Reinforced, they renewed their demonstrations the next night, and a severe engagement followed, in which a dozen or more persons were seriously wounded. The next day the negroes wisely resolved to pull up stakes and return to their respective homes, to meditate on the love of their fellow Ohio men. But the hearts of the white Republican patriots were fired against the man and brother; and as the colored people, men, women and children, were the next day passing through the streets of Danville, on foot, on horseback, in wagons, fleeing the wrath to come, they were fired upon with muskets, rifles, shot-guns, and pistols, and the Lord only knows how many of them were killed and how many were wounded.

"This outlines a terrible story and a true one. It is compiled from Ohio newspapers. It is a story of race prejudice, of outrage, of crime, of murder. It comes from the home of Hayes and Sheman and Garfield. It is not coupled with information that any arrests have been made, or that steps towards arrests have been taken, or that the federal power is to be invoked for the protection of the negroes. It is the plain story of a brutal and cowardly crime, perpetrated on the sacred soil of Ohio with impunity."

Bravo, Mr. Argus! Your description of the outrage is well done, and if sincere, does credit to your humanity; and we must hasten to relieve your sympathetic heart by assuring you that some arrests have been made, and there is a prospect of some at least of the guilty parties receiving punishment. You will no doubt also be glad to learn that one of the whites engaged in the outrage which has so roused your "righteous indignation," has since died of his wounds. But how will it intensify your anguish and wring your inmost soul, when we inform you that Danville, the scene of all this violence and outrage, which you have so vividly portrayed, is the great Democratic stronghold—the Gibraltar, so to speak—of Democracy in this county! For proof of this, let us refer you to a few official election returns, (a "fair count," and not on the "Alabama plan").

BOUND OVER. GUS DICKMAN, JAKE WHITE AND FRANK MANKER, FOR PARTICIPATING IN THE DAN- VILLE RIOT. EVIDENCE SHOWING THAT FIF- TEEN OR TWENTY ROUGHS ATTACKED THE COLORED FOLKS THAT SATURDAY NIGHT.
The preliminary examination of some of the parties engaged in the recent disgraceful camp meeting riot at Danville, which has been postponed from time to time, was held before Mayor Beeson last Thursday afternoon, in the Court House. R. T. Hough, Esq., and R. M. Dittey, of Lynchburg, appeared for the defense, and Prosecuting Attorney Hire, and Cyrus Newby, Esq., and Judge Doan, of Wilmington, for the State. The affidavit was sworn out by A. G. Mallory, the Wilmington preacher, against Gus Dickman, Wm. Dickman, Jake White, Frank Manker, Wm. Eggling, and others to the affiant unknown, charging them with riotously disturbing a religious meeting, by throwing stones, swearing and shooting, on Saturday night, July 24th, 1880.

Gus Dickman, Wake white and Frank Manker were present to answer to the charge, Eggling not having been arrested, and Bill Dickman being dead. The defendants pleaded not guilty, and the examination of the State's witnesses began, which consumed most of the afternoon.

The evidence given did not differ materially from the facts published in the News, at the time of the occurrence, except in one particular. The News, in its report, stated that there were only five men, whose names are mentioned in the affidavit, that engaged in the attack on Saturday night, but all the evidence given shows that there were in fact all the way from fifteen to forty, while there were only twelve or thirteen of the colored men. All the witnesses agreed that the attack was begun by the whites, and that they fired first.

After the State rested their case, the defense made a motion to discharge, and submitted it without introducing any evidence. Mayor Beeson overruled the motion, and bound the defendants over to the Probate Court in the sum of $300 each, which, being given, they were discharged.

Albanian volunteers for service in Thessaly and Epirus.

At the election to the Council General in France the Republicans have returned 704 candidates and the Conservatives 281.

The Bojana, an influential Italian association, have decided to agitate for an international exhibition to be held at Rome in 1885 and 1886.

At Woodland Mills, Tenn., yesterday, Henry Crenshaw was shot in the breast and mortally wounded at the Owl House by Alex. Elison. The crowd is pursuing Elison and will lynch him if caught.

A terrific thunder storm prevailed Sunday night in and about Chicago. Considerable damage is reported from lightning in Illinois, Wisconsin, Indiana and Michigan. Numerous barns were struck and burned with grain.

The Russian authorities at Novarossik, in the Black Sea, fired on a vessel conveying thither some Greek and Armenian emigrants and prevented their landing, killing several of them. A Russian man-of-war subsequently captured the vessel and imprisoned the passengers and crew.

The schooner Tom Boy sprang aleak Sunday morning while on its way to Chicago from Haighton, with a cargo of powder. The negro boy who killed the son of Thomas Devine, in Trinity county.
the negro boy, who killed the son of Thomas Devine, in Trinity county, some weeks ago, was taken from jail the other day and hung. He was too young to suffer judicial punishment, and the fact being proven that he wilfully killed the little boy, it is supposed, lead to this violence on the part of a mob.

Jones and to the officers and men of the frontier battalion for their efforts in the protection of the frontier against Mexican and Indian raids, and the arrest and return to justice of lawless white men.

A charming Dallas widow went to Weatherford, and put up at White's Hotel. Mrs. White, like a good housewife, thoroughly inspected the house at night, and when she invaded the room of this same charming widow she was thunderstruck to find her liege lord in there with her. There was a scene and a separation, and the field was left, as it usually is, to a widow.

At Fort Worth an attempt was made to deliver one Kendrick, convicted of cattle stealing, from the jail. The vigilance of the guard prevented, and afterward, when Sheriff Henderson was attacked while crossing the court house yard with the prisoner, he knocked one man down who drew a pistol upon him, and then took him into the jail. Jordan, Maj. A. H. Swanson and J. Waldo, of the Central railroad; Col. John Seely, of the G. H. & H. railroad, were present. A revision of the tariff is supposed to be the object of the meeting.

The Concho Times says: "Mrs. Isabella Storey, a patient from Kerr county, died at the State Lunatic Asylum, at Austin, a few days ago, of inflammation of the brain. She was the daughter of Capt. George Simmons, a wealthy merchant of Plymouth, Massachusetts, and a native of that state. Her father had cast her off from his household; and, previous to her being sent to the asylum, she had lived here in destitute circumstances."

Houston Post: "The Galveston News is a fine paper, very. There is no use disputing that. But don't the News think it is time to take down the rusty hyperpole it flies at the masthead, that the circulation of the News is equal to that of all the other daily papers in the state combined? The News ought to know that we can mention three cities outside of Galveston the aggregate of whose newspapers daily published would be in excess of the News considerably. What is the use, then, of harping on a string that doesn't sound."

Marshall Messenger: Bonner, who murdered Wheeler, an editor, in the streets of Paris, about a year ago, is to be tried at Cooper, Delta county, on the ninth of August. This was a case of open assassination. The murderer had no reasonable excuse for his act. He was not even drunk. Yet he was admitted to bail. The press had very little to say about this judicial outrage, and if he is acquitted, a majority of the journals that made so much fuss over Currie's case will probably dismiss the matter with a paragraph. So much for the consistency of blatherskite Texas journalism.

The woman murdered in a tent along with her companion, Hodges, near Morgan, some weeks ago, turns out to be Mrs. Howard, the wife of a Dallas county farmer, named R. P. Howard. In 1867 he married Miss Mattie White, by whom he had one child, a boy. His wife became a loose woman, and left him to live with one Levi Wilson, and then with the man Hodges, with whom she was in bed. Two little girls, born after she began her life of shame, supposed to be the children of Wilson, were left in the camp beside the dead mother. Such is the end of a wife and mother forgetful of all that is held most sacred and pure in society.

The Express gives the following account of the killing at Eagle Pass of John Zoller by Sheriff Beacom: "John had been drinking, and Beacom was endeavoring to arrest a disorderly man when Zoller and Judge Ware appeared upon the scene in a buggy. Beacom said something about raising a posse to assist him in making the arrest, when Zoller exclaimed, 'posse be d—d! I'll take the man myself.' John did so, and afterwards walked up to Beacom and charged him with cowardice. Beacom remonstrated, the writer says, but 'John kept on crowding him until Beacom shot him in the breast. In the meantime Beacom stumbled, and one of the crowd cried, 'now, John, give it to him,' but while getting up Beacom shot him again in the bowels, and started to shoot him again, when one of the crowd called on him to hold up, it was enough. John then leaned up against one of the posts in front of the court house and said, 'Beacom, that's enough; you have shot me through the heart.' Beacom was put under arrest and afterward released on a $1500 bond. John died about noon of the oth at the post hospital. He had a decent burial, and many friends followed the remains to their long resting place."

On the evening of the 5th inst., Woodson L. Gunnels, a well-to-do farmer living 20 miles west of Americus, Ga., left home to visit a sick neighbor and returning home at ten o'clock at night, found his wife and nine of his ten small children in a horrible sleep from the effects of morphine administered in lemonade by Mrs. Gunnels. reed-evans-pennington-1880-08-02.A7: In Trinity county, Texas, a little white boy, aged about twelve years, the son of Mr. Dwire was hoeing in the field in company with two negroes, when a third negro boy, Bud Evans, sixteen years old, approached the parties at work, armed with an Enfield gun, and one of the negroes remarked: "Here's Bud. BURTON, August 17,

BURTON, August 17,
Editors Banner:

Greenvine the capital of precinct No. 6, has been the scene of a very deplorable action. About three weeks ago several farmers missed some of their cattle, but a search proved fruitless. At last some of the cattle, 11 head, were found to have been sold by two negroes, Rube Carothers and Andrew Jackson, to a butcher at New Ulm. Mr. Chas. Limbacker, owner of said cattle identified 9 of the hides by the brands and also found a cow and calf in the pasture.

Rube Carothers was arrested under a warrant issued by justice Campbell, of Greenvine, in Austin county and had a preliminary examination, after which he was sent to the Brenham jail for safe keeping. He claimed to have bought the cattle and proposed to prove it. Andrew Jackson, Rube's pal is still at large. About the same time it became known that the negroes had sold 3 large steers to a Rutersville butcher. At New Ulm Carothers had given a bill of sale as Williams and at Rutersville as Geo. Peel. He promised to take more cattle to Rutersville next day, but was prevented by his arrest.

On Monday he was taken from Brenham to Greenvine and had a preliminary examination when the facts above were fully proven. During the trial the prisoner behaved in a most outrageous manner, cursing the court and bystanders; the constable was compelled to tie him, but he continued his abuse and court was adjourned till next day. He was placed in the hands of a special constable, who fearing violence, carried, after the crowd had despersed, the prisoner to a rent house in the vicinity for safe keeping, during the night the prisoner was taken by a disguised mob, carried about three-quarters of a mile and hung to a cottonwood tree.

As much as such occurrences are to be deplored they are the natural outgrowth of a low standard of morals of a large portion of our population, and of our criminal law system which makes the punishment of a criminal a matter of great uncertainty. He had been arrested and tried before upon a similar charge, but by having the necessary swearing done in his behalf escaped justice. He boasted while a prisoner that he would be punished by only a few years in the penitentiary and when out he would resume "business"; he also told the officer that as soon as he got out "he would thin out those who had brought him to grief." Great credit is due deputy sheriff Ligon, of Fayette county, and constable Williams, of this beat, for working up the case and arresting Rube Carothers. H. R. V. B.

rube-caruthers-brenham-1880-08-17.A11:
The Lynch.
GREENVINE, Tex., August 21., '80.
Reuben Carothers, colored, had been undergoing a preliminary examination in my court on the 16th inst., on a charge of theft of stock; at dark 5 witnesses had been examined for the state, one for the state and two for the defendant were yet to examine. The evidence before the court up to adjournment went to show that the defendant had been guilty of selling, aided by two other colored men, 15 head of cattle that had been stolen in this precinct. The cattle were valued at $220 00. The defendant was arrested and brought before me on the 12th inst.; the trial was postponed to give defendant a chance to procure counsel and the evidence of two important witnesses. The defendant waived the right of a bond for his appearance. He was lodged in jail until the 16th. Sheriff Ligon consented at the request of the court to write down the evidence taken during the trial; the prisoner conducted himself badly; he showed no respect for the court, and insulted the witnesses, cursing and swearing. The court bore the insults for it was manifest that the prisoner was intoxicated. On inquiry as to how he got the spirits I was informed that on leaving Brenham, deputy sheriff Jack Lands, at the request of the prisoner, furnished him a half pint flask of whiskey. The court adjourned till 8 o'clock next morning and Wm. Brandt deputised to take charge of the prisoner, bring him to court next morning. Mr. Brandt summoned three parties to assist him guard the prisoner. From their report about a quarter to 11 o'clock in the night, about 50 masked men suddenly charged on them, taking the prisoner by force and carried him away; his body was found about 9 o'clock next morning hanging to a cottonwood tree in Labahia prairie. An inquest was held, 5 witnesses examined and evidence reduced to writing.

I am informed that some of the friends of deceased are disposed to cast reflections on my official conduct in the premises. To such I would state that my conscience is easy of having done nothing wrong, either legally or morally. If there was an organized mob in waiting when court adjourned I was ignorant of it; I was forced to adjourn court on account of the conduct of the intoxicated prisoner.

As to the justifiacation or condemnation of the act above referred so, I leave it with the people to draw their own inference.

C. G. CAMPBELL.

THE VERDICT.—We, the jury find that the deceased came to his death by being hung to a cottonwood tree in Labahia prairie; by the neck with a new grass rope, unknown to us.

SAM ARNETT,
ALLEN TAYLOR,
S. S. REDFORD,
S. T. WOOD,
L. A. CAMPBELL,
Y. W. BOON,
CAMPBELL,
P.W.C., Precinct No. 6.

DURING a riot between Catholics and Orangemen at Dungannon, Ireland, on Sunday, the 15th, the police first used buckshot and then ball cartridges to disperse the crowd, who returned the fire with revolvers. Many persons were wounded. At Down Patrick the Catholics and Orangemen fought for several hours, a number on both sides being severely wounded; and at Belfast a similar collision occurred, two deaths resulting.

A WEDDING party at Painesville, O., were poisoned at supper, evidently by some deleterious substance being mixed with the food. All who partook were seriously ill, some of them nigh to death, but all will recover.

TWENTY-ONE persons have been tried by court-martial and convicted at Kief, Russia, for political offenses. Two were sentenced to death, three to twenty years' imprisonment, and sixteen to hard labor for terms varying from ten to fifteen years.

DURING a drunken carousal at the house of John Kelleher, in Oakland, Cal., the house was set on fire and two of his children were burned to death and a third was fatally injured. Mrs. Kelleher and another woman, Mrs. King, were both badly burned, and Kelleher was slightly scorched.

THE Yaeger Mill at St. Louis, the largest flouring mill in the city, was totally destroyed by fire on the night of the 17th. Total loss about $450,000; insurance, $285,-000.

EUREKA, Nevada, has had another disastrous fire, which swept over about the same ground as the fire of a year ago. A large number of business buildings and private residences were destroyed. The losses will aggregate nearly $1,000,000.

GENERAL BRYAN GRIMES, a well known citizen of North Carolina, was assassinated near his home in Pitt County by some person unknown. He was shot dead while driving along the road.

While a circus procession was taking place at Winchester, Va., on the 16th, Andrew Drayton, the keeper of the hyenas, who was occupying the cage of those animals, was set upon by them and almost literally devoured before he could be rescued. His injuries were thought to be fatal.

Frost appeared in Central New York on the night of August 15, and at one place in Delaware County ice formed.

Floods swept down the glen of Glendore, County Donegal, Ireland, flooding the church at Commienon and drowning eleven persons, who were carried away by the rush of waters.

A MOVEMENT has been set on foot for inducing immigration to West Tennessee. A society has been organized at Memphis, under the auspices of the State Bureau of Immigration.

LUKE BLACKBURN won the one mile and a half race at Long Branch, on the 17th, in the unprecedented time of 2:34.

A CASE of twenty rifles, shipped from Muford for Cork, was seized by the police.

A MAN named Marburger, a traveling salesman for the tobacco house of Abel Brothers, Denver, was found dead in a house of bad repute in that city on the morning of the 19th. There had been a quarrel the previous night, in which the keeper of the house, Carrie Smith, struck Marburger over the head with a bottle, and a male friend of hers then clubbed him with a revolver. The murdered man leaves a wife and three children.

At Norfolk, Va., Mrs. Elizabeth Benson, mother of Chief of Police Benson, who committed suicide in January last, on the 19th cut her throat and then jumped into a hogshead of water. When found she was dead.

JOSHUA BALLARD, City Marshal of Ennis, Texas, was shot and killed on the morning of the 19th by S. B. Alexander, whom he had arrested and locked up for being drunk and disorderly on the previous night.

REUBEN CARUTHERS, a colored cattle thief, was lynched near Brenham, Texas, on the night of the 18th.

EX-GOV. HERSCHEL V. JOHNSON, of Georgia, died on the 16th, at his residence in Jefferson County, aged 68.

The bombardment of Candahar began on the 19th. Cannonading was kept up during the entire day on three sides of the city, but without inflicting any serious damage.

Two Mexicans, named Gallegh and Valdez, arrested at Albuquerque, N. M., a few days ago on suspicion of murder, have made a full confession. The name of the man murdered was S. Daprez, and it appeared he had been a sheep-owner in Southern Colorado. They said they obtained $1,200 in money, a check for $125, several Post-office orders, two horses and a wagon, and other effects. Of the money $406 was found on their persons. Duprez was traveling south alone, and stopped in a tent over night. One of the Mexicans shot him while asleep, while the other stood by with an ax ready to afford assistance if necessary.

A party of Russian emigrants, sixty-seven in number, the sole survivors of a party of three hundred and thirty, which left Russia in 1877 for Brazil, have arrived at New York sick and destitute. They found the South American climate unsuited to them, and after losing nearly all their funds decided to leave the country where they had experienced so many hardships.

Dr. Turner, Secretary of the National Board of Health, says that from official reports received from what are known as the yellow fever districts, he does not anticipate that there will be any yellow fever in this country this season in an epidemic form. There may be sporadic cases, but the disease would then be confined and would not spread. He said the most dangerous part of the season is already over, and nothing that could indicate the breaking out of a yellow fever epidemic has been reported. He attributes the freedom of Memphis from the fever this year to her establishment of sewerage and other sanitary precautions against the engenderment of the disease. The officers of the Board in the different sections are ready to act at a moment's notice to the extent of the power conferred upon them by law. THE Indian Agent at Poplar River.
